description: CornCon X talks from CornCon X 2024.

talks.title: HIdden Dangers of AI in Devloper Workflows
talks.teaser: Dwayne McDaniel Sr. investigates HIdden Dangers of AI in Devloper Workflows.
talks.summary:
Overview: Dwayne McDaniel presents at CornCon-X on hidden dangers of AI in developer workflows, focusing on human factors rather than technical jailbreaks or prompt injection.

Key Topics: AI tools enabling developers to act without thinking; the Butlerian Jihad concept of increasing actions without cognition; risks of over-reliance on AI-assisted development; and why human judgment remains essential.

Technical Details: McDaniel draws on Frank Herbert's Dune reference about machines increasing actions done without thinking, arguing AI coding assistants create similar risks where developers ship code they don't fully understand.

Takeaways: AI development tools risk degrading developer critical thinking. Teams should maintain code comprehension standards and resist shipping AI-generated code without human review and understanding.

talks.title: The SaaS and The Furious
talks.teaser: Ryan Wisniewski details The SaaS and The Furious.
talks.summary:
SaaS Breach Trends

Obsidian threat operations lead Ryan Wizoski reframes “The SaaS and the Furious” beyond business-email-compromise clichés. Publicly disclosed SaaS compromises follow a steep upward curve—about 220 cases in the current year at talk time—because SaaS concentrates data while security often lags migration.

Identity-First Adversary Model

Roughly 90% of cases he handles stem from identity compromise rather than exposed APIs. SaaS search, export, and download features become reconnaissance and exfiltration tools; his fastest case went from initial access to full data theft in nine minutes. Average Microsoft tenants show about 1,000 OAuth grants, ~90% unused in 90 days—massive forgotten integration risk.

Hands-On Cloud Intrusion Style

Attackers skip traditional network mapping; they log in and click application tiles. Free SaaS trials let operators train on authentic UIs without victim hardware. Wizoski organizes observed tactics by application type and urges visibility across every integration, user, and fourth/fifth-party dependency—not just primary productivity suites.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Ryan Wisniewski, Threat Operations Lead at Obsidian Security, examines the escalating surge of enterprise Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) compromises. Presenting at CornCon, Wisniewski debunks the misconception that SaaS threats are confined to traditional Business Email Compromise (BEC), demonstrating how attackers exploit the SaaS ecosystem to execute rapid reconnaissance, persistent access, and data exfiltration. Drawing on telemetry from hundreds of real-world enterprise breaches, he outlines prevalent attacker kill chains, identity abuse techniques, and essential detection strategies.

Key Topics:
- SaaS compromise landscape and the collapse of traditional network perimeters
- Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing and non-human identity / OAuth sprawl
- Persistence via rogue MFA registration and defense evasion via inbox rules
- Rapid data exfiltration mechanics and helpdesk social engineering kill chains

Technical Details:
Wisniewski tracks over 220 publicly disclosed enterprise SaaS breaches, highlighting that modern attackers rarely rely on zero-day API exploits against platforms like Salesforce, Microsoft 365, or Workday. Instead, approximately 90% of compromises stem directly from identity compromise. A major unmanaged attack surface is non-human identity and OAuth application sprawl: the average enterprise tenant contains roughly 1,000 OAuth application grants, with over 90% remaining inactive for more than 90 days, providing unmonitored backdoors into corporate data. Attackers gain initial access primarily through Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) reverse proxy phishing, which intercepts session tokens and bypasses traditional multi-factor authentication (MFA), often targeting unmanaged employee mobile devices lacking Mobile Device Management (MDM).

Once inside, attackers establish persistence in approximately 85% of investigated cases by registering their own rogue software-based MFA device (such as an Okta Verify or Microsoft Authenticator instance) within the compromised user profile. Because identity providers (IdPs) permit selecting the destination device for push notifications, attackers route future MFA prompts to their own hardware, completely bypassing the legitimate employee. For defense evasion, adversaries create targeted email forwarding and mailbox rules. Rather than deleting notifications or marking them as read (which easily triggers basic alert rules), attackers program rules to divert login alerts, password resets, and payroll correspondence into default system folders that users rarely monitor, such as RSS Subscriptions or Conversation History.

During the discovery phase, attackers systematically browse single sign-on (SSO) app tiles to enumerate enterprise permissions, often utilizing stolen session tokens concurrently from multiple geographical IP addresses and user agents. Native SaaS search, export, and sharing capabilities facilitate rapid data exfiltration; in one documented financial sector breach, an attacker compromised an executive account and simply updated top-level OneDrive permissions to "share publicly," allowing unauthorized bulk downloads via external guest accounts. Wisniewski observes that the elapsed time between initial access and complete enterprise data exfiltration has dropped to as little as nine minutes. Furthermore, attackers actively abuse Self-Service Password Reset (SSPR) workflows combined with telecommunication SIM-swapping, as well as social engineering IT helpdesks using copycat MGM-style vishing techniques.

Key Takeaways:
Enterprises must shift detection focus from network perimeters to identity and SaaS telemetry, establishing continuous monitoring for rogue MFA device registrations and anomalous session token reuse across disparate geographic locations. Organizations must conduct automated audits of dormant OAuth integrations and revoke unutilized third-party permissions. Migrating away from SMS-based OTP toward FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware tokens and enforcing device compliance via MDM effectively mitigates AiTM reverse-proxy phishing and SIM-swapping attacks.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Alarmed & Dangerous: Exploiting Vulns in EMS Systems, McKeegan Curran, TAPS Team, Caterpillar
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Alarmed & Dangerous: Exploiting Vulns in EMS Systems, McKeegan Curran, TAPS Team, Caterpillar.
talks.summary:
Discovery via a Fraternity Fire Panel

Keegan Curran found a critical IDOR while proxying his fraternity's upgraded fire-alarm mobile app with Fiddler. Changing the site-number parameter in API calls returned other customers' data within minutes, despite the app's outdated codebase and infrequent security updates.

Exposed Sensitive Data

Vulnerable responses leaked customer addresses, lockbox combinations, and digital-lock codes for fire and security systems. Because POST, PUT, and DELETE were equally affected, attackers could modify—not just view—remote system state without authentication beyond a valid app session.

Abuse Scenarios at Scale

Curran mapped roughly 597 vulnerable sites in Davenport, over 14,000 in Iowa, and 269,000 across North America including hospitals, schools, power plants, and Fortune 50 facilities. Attackers could trigger immediate emergency dispatch, place alarms in test mode to suppress real events, or induce alarm fatigue before physical intrusion.

Remediation Timeline

Reported in July 2024 through a local intermediary because the vendor lacked a formal bug-bounty program, the vendor patched quickly given the potential for mass false dispatches and critical-infrastructure impact. The talk underscores how overlooked physical-security SaaS APIs can threaten public safety.

talks.title: An alternate ending to Star Wars and how you mitigate risk, John Aron, CEO, Aronetics
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of An alternate ending to Star Wars and how you mitigate risk, John Aron, CEO, Aronetics.
talks.summary:
Star Wars as risk metaphor

John Aron, CEO of Aronetics and adviser to the Joint Applied Task Force supporting USSOCOM, uses Star Wars imagery to discuss federal cyber risk mitigation. He blends personal near-death experience, Equifax-scale breach context, and skepticism toward vendor hype about trillion-dollar cyber "opportunities" while major hacks continue.

Identity and breach reality

Aron argues consumers maintain plural online identities yet cannot trust breached credit bureaus to protect them. He frames cyber defense as navigating fog-of-war, citing FBI guidance that defenders face two categories of organizations: those hacked and those that do not yet know it.

Defense in depth via fighters

He maps X-Wing layered defenses versus agile TIE fighters—speed and maneuverability without implicit channel security—to different mitigation strategies. Open-source intelligence revealing the Death Star exhaust-port flaw illustrates how adversaries find single points of failure when layered controls are bypassed.

talks.title: Winning the Game of Active Directory, Brandon Colley, Sr. Security Consultant
talks.teaser: Walks through common Active Directory attacks, from anonymous enumeration to certificate abuse, with the matching defensive fixes.
talks.summary:
The talk uses a pre-built, intentionally vulnerable Active Directory lab, framed as a game with four levels: reconnaissance, enumeration and privilege escalation, and finally taking over the domain. The speaker, who moved into security from systems administration, runs each attack and then shows how to close the same weakness. Early steps include anonymous read access that exposed a password in a user description field, username guessing through Kerberos responses, AS-REP roasting of accounts without pre-authentication, and password spraying with credential stuffing.

The middle levels cover Kerberoasting of service accounts with stale service principal names, LLMNR poisoning with Responder and NTLM relay for local admin access, and BloodHound paths that abuse Group Policy permissions. Pass-the-hash against a shared local administrator password reaches a domain controller, and unconstrained delegation allows ticket reuse. The final level abuses an unpatched Print Spooler through PrintNightmare and misconfigured AD CS certificate templates (ESC1) to dump the domain database.

For each case the speaker lists fixes: removing anonymous access, longer usernames, disabling LLMNR, enforcing NTLMv2, enabling LDAP signing, deploying LAPS, moving to constrained delegation, flagging admin accounts as sensitive, turning off the Print Spooler on domain controllers, and using Locksmith to find risky templates. The closing message is that Active Directory security keeps changing, so regular assessments matter.

talks.title: From Burnout to Balance, Steve Shelton, CEO, Green Shoe Consulting
talks.teaser: Explains how stress turns into burnout for security workers and offers two quick techniques to calm down in the moment.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's path from football and corporate sales into research on stress and burnout in cyber security. He defines stress as a response, separates threat from challenge, and describes burnout as a reaction to chronic stressors that have not been managed. He cites Gallup-based figures suggesting about one in three workers is disengaged, notes that security leaders often stay in a role for under two years, and puts the cost of replacing an employee at roughly 30 to 40 percent of salary.

He then presents survey figures from a global CISO survey, where 71 percent of respondents were concerned about significant stress on their personal health and 59 percent were worried about burnout. Stressors he lists include sacrifice syndrome, layoffs, poor managers, unnecessary meetings and unrealistic expectations. Burnout comes from a mismatch in six areas: workload, autonomy, community, fairness, values and reward. Its symptoms are exhaustion, cynicism and professional inefficacy. He argues that organizational design adds pressure on top of personal coping, and that the most common request from employees is a private, confidential place to talk.

For the practical part, he walks the room through a breathing pattern with a longer exhale and a progressive relaxation exercise that tenses and releases the fist and forearm. He also covers the stoplight model of performance, personal response plans, and recovery through sleep, movement and eating. The takeaway is to notice your own state, plan for known triggers, and rebuild habits in small steps rather than expecting a quick fix.

talks.title: The Cyber Threat Landscape: What's Next? Paige Hanson, Co-Founder, SecureLabs
talks.teaser: Surveys everyday scams and emerging threats, from mail theft and QR codes to AI voice cloning and ransomware.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys how everyday scams have changed. It opens with old-school crime that still happens, including mail theft, purse theft, check washing and shoulder surfing on public Wi-Fi. Digital tactics follow: smishing texts that imitate banks, tax agencies and delivery services, and voice spoofing that fakes a caller ID so a relative seems to be in trouble. A family passphrase is suggested as a check.

Phishing and business email compromise come next, along with QR code abuse such as stickers pasted over parking-meter codes and brushing, where unsolicited gifts prompt a scan. FBI-reported QR scam losses reached $150 million in 2023. Ransomware is described as more aggressive, with demands sized to cyber insurance limits and double extortion that also targets clients. Layered controls, restricted access, tested backups and incident response plans that assume extended downtime are recommended. AI adds polished phishing emails, a note-taking tool that emailed a private call transcript, and cloned voices built from 10 to 15 seconds of audio.

The close covers oversharing, from photo locations to neighborhood posts that reveal routines. Practical steps include disabling auto-connect on public Wi-Fi, using a VPN and password manager, enabling MFA starting with email and bank accounts, and reporting scams through usa.gov.

talks.title: My First Year as a Pen Tester, Alexis Diediker, OCO Consultant, ProCircular
talks.teaser: A newcomer offensive consultant shares a chaotic first year of certs, client tests, and lessons for aspiring penetration testers.
talks.summary:
The presenter describes leaving a non-technical background and obsessive self-study to join ProCircular as an intern in May 2023, where expectations from school and labs collided with real engagements. Early weeks included uncomfortable vishing and rapid exposure to tools outside the classroom; a certification bargain with leadership tied Net+, Security+, and PNPT to a pentester track rather than defaulting to help desk or SOC work.

Through 2023 and 2024 the narrative covers shadowing senior testers, failing and retaking exams, SANS Cyber Academy work, Q4 compliance rush, and being told to run an external bank test before feeling ready—forgetting basics under pressure yet delivering a happy client. March onward brought awkward client debriefs, humility when Hack The Box skills did not transfer, red-team social angles, a failed then passed CRTO, and promotion to consultant, with emphasis on documenting findings precisely for customers.

Closing advice treats every engagement as learning, urges pushing into uncomfortable techniques without hammering dead ends, and stresses scripting, organization, and continuous skill refresh. Q&A extends into TryHackMe and Hack The Box for curious IT staff, a live ntdsutil win after Secret Dump failed, GraphRunner for cloud paths, and a call to reduce gatekeeping in offensive security culture.

talks.teaser: Build trust with teams while mapping access, prioritizing risks and planning for automation that people can maintain.
talks.summary: The speaker describes identity access management as an ongoing effort to inventory employee, contractor, client and vendor access, then shape access around roles and business needs. He outlines how to gather information through conversations with staff, address their pain points, assess practical risks and involve department representatives in reviewing tools and decisions. Attendees learn why automation needs realistic expectations, ongoing maintenance and dedicated staff time.

talks.title: AI is killing my company culture
talks.teaser: Chris Johnson investigates AI is killing my company culture.
talks.summary: Chris Johnson, a CompTIA security director, argues generative AI adoption can poison workplace culture when rolled out without governance. Survey data shows heavy vendor AI marketing while employees smuggle free chatbots despite corporate bans, leaking data to public models. He walks through shadow IT, Grammarly and Copilot licensing traps, and a help-desk firm that enabled Copilot harassment classifiers overnight, briefly flagging normal banter as toxic until policies and etiquette training retuned the detections. Johnson recommends NIST AI risk framing, tight acceptable-use rules, containerized enterprise tools, vendor questionnaires about model data flows, and leadership champions who can enforce boundaries before litigation arrives.

talks.title: Let's do that Time Warp again! Messages for better learning, Michael Odell, Consultant, ProCircular
talks.teaser: A consultant outlines a low-cost, self-driven path into security using Obsidian, atomic notes, and free learning resources.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames a problem many aspiring practitioners face: formal degrees, boot camps, and certifications can be expensive and age quickly, while generic advice to “take this course” does not scale. He proposes a long-lived, self-directed curriculum inspired by open university-style outlines and metalearning principles, aimed at pentesting and broader technical growth without heavy debt.

The middle of the session is a hands-on tour of Obsidian as a personal knowledge base. He advocates atomic notes and evergreen notes that you revise as understanding changes, then links ideas with Kanban for project tracking, Excalidraw for visual maps, and Dataview to assemble resource webs programmatically—useful when a live engagement surfaces a topic you documented long ago. Around that workflow he maps cheap or free learning sources: college syllabi hunted online, MIT OpenCourseWare, YouTube, GitHub, Hack The Box, and picoCollege’s staged belt-style certifications, while noting that traditional school can still help with structure, networking, and résumé filters.

He closes on habits: follow community channels and conference content for continuing education, expect repeated failure while practicing, gamify progress with time tracking and streaks, and break large goals into small rewarded tasks. Q&A covers prioritizing competing study topics, splitting old monolithic notes, judging what deserves capture, and treating vault files as plain markdown searchable with standard tools.

talks.title: Strategic Endpoint Hardening with CIS, Zach Kromkowski, Co-Founder, Senteon
talks.teaser: Shows why Windows endpoints drift from CIS hardening guidance and how to plan, deploy and verify settings.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why Windows endpoints so often stay in insecure default states and how the CIS Benchmarks can guide hardening. The speaker explains that CIS publishes prioritized controls and far more granular benchmarks, and that the Windows 11 benchmark runs to roughly 1,300 pages covering about 470 settings. Only around 15 percent of those settings, about 70, are configured securely out of the box, so most machines are left at not configured.

The middle of the talk covers native tooling. Group Policy, Intune and PowerShell can all change settings, but changes may fail to apply, conflict with local policy, or revert later, and Intune mainly pushes policy without checking the result. Reporting and verification are manual at scale. The speaker also describes a working group that mapped CIS safeguards to controls, where control 4 alone has 43 safeguards, and notes that hardening changes can disrupt applications that depend on the settings.

The closing advice is a practical plan: choose a framework, define the assets in scope, assess them with a scanner, remediate the highest-value settings first, monitor and verify changes, and report results. Practitioners should aim for standardized configurations, start small, and be ready to explain the business benefit. The speaker also points out that CIS provides crosswalks to frameworks such as PCI and HIPAA, which can make audits easier.

talks.title: Turning The Tables: Using Breach Data, Jacob Esparza, Sr. Manager, Global Threat Intelligence PWC
talks.teaser: Shows how stolen breach data and infostealer logs can be pivoted to unmask cybercriminals and map their infrastructure.
talks.summary:
Jacob Esparza starts by defining breach data as information taken without permission and later exposed, sold or shared. He surveys where it appears, including forums, Telegram channels, paste sites, code repositories and infostealer malware logs, and argues that malware logs are among the best sources for unmasking actors. He advises against buying stolen data, since the seller may be sanctioned.

Most of the talk walks through cases. An extortion victim's threat actor was traced to the UK within a day, which led to a police visit. A Moroccan actor's handle appeared in several logs from one machine, where saved form fields revealed an address and email accounts that led to a name. A Vietnamese actor was linked through a reused email, a domain registration record and a Facebook photo. A carding-related actor's credentials pointed to a company and its owner's LinkedIn profile. Usernames from one log also tied separate forum accounts together.

He closes with cautions: a log entry does not prove ownership, investigative leads are not evidence and may not be admissible in court, and analysts should protect their own identities and plan storage and legal review. Distinctive selectors and patient pivoting drive the work.

talks.title: The Plains Have Eyes: Mass Surveillance in the Hawkeye State, Hendrik van Pelt
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for The Plains Have Eyes: Mass Surveillance in the Hawkeye State, Hendrik van Pelt.
talks.summary: Hendrik van Pelt maps Flock Safety camera pods that appeared along his suburban Iowa drive to return Amazon packages. Chapter-twenty-two records requests reveal dozens of ALPR devices in neighboring cities, million-dollar contracts, and a SaaS platform that fingerprints vehicles beyond plate text. He explains how agencies share detections nationwide, how vendors retain hardware on public poles while billing municipalities for storm damage, and how Clive police withheld rally attendance footage by labeling it investigative intelligence. The talk argues pervasive private surveillance lacks security audits or meaningful transparency, cites vendor marketing about live overwatch during traffic stops, and urges residents to press councils and fund legal challenges.

talks.title: Building Tabletop Exercises for Your Company, Barry Suskind, Director, Docent Institute
talks.teaser: Explains how to design, run and report on tabletop exercises that test both technical teams and executives during a breach.
talks.summary:
The talk covers why tabletop exercises matter: simulated breaches that expose gaps in networks, systems, applications and in how teams work together. The speaker, who has run them for about ten years, began by joining exercises led by outside incident response firms that felt unrealistic and dry, and then started writing his own scenarios. He separates three formats: technical exercises for security and operations staff, business exercises for executives, risk and legal teams that begin once a breach has been declared, and combined sessions that bring everyone into one room.

Preparation takes most of the effort. He recommends updating the incident response plan, confirming that key personnel and listed technology are still current, and scheduling sessions months ahead around vacations and production releases. Scenarios are fed to participants as timed injects. One example starts with an application host contacting an unknown internet address, which leads to finding unrestricted outbound traffic and, in a software scan, about 15 applications still running an Apache Ant version untouched since 2012. Another follows a Mac user whose documents disappear, showing that the cloud sync was not covering Mac desktop and document folders.

Common pitfalls include vendor-run exercises that do not understand the environment, no-shows, side conversations, and executives who dismiss plausible scenarios. The after-action report should list gaps candidly, while its executive summary highlights what went well. Corrective actions need named owners, deadlines and follow-up, or they tend never to get fixed.

talks.title: The Worst Career Advice I Ever Heard, Ira Winkler, CISO, CYE Security
talks.teaser: Argues cyber security careers rest on fundamentals, credentials and adjacent experience, and warns against easy-entry career advice.
talks.summary:
Ira Winkler opens with frustration at misleading career advice online, such as claims that a CISSP guarantees lifelong employment or that no degree, programming or experience is needed. He notes that entry-level security openings are scarce and that employers still screen for basic networking knowledge. His own route, from an early wish to become an astronaut to programming at the NSA, shows that security is a specialty built on other computing disciplines.

On education and credentials, he argues that a degree signals the ability to show up and finish assigned work, even though the major itself is a small share of the credits. Advanced degrees mainly prepare people for research or academia. Certifications show that an outside party judged the holder qualified and that the person invested effort, though they do not prove competence. He also stresses programming, basic math such as binary and hexadecimal, and clear writing, since a penetration tester who cannot explain fixes adds little value.

For getting hired, he recommends taking an adjacent role such as system administration or project management and moving into security once that experience is in place. He favors networking over submitting applications into automated filters, suggests rewording existing IT work to show its security content, and advises ignoring online influencers who sell shortcuts. His closing point is to be wary of anyone who tells you what you do not need.

talks.title: The Privacy Paradox, Adriana Antunes Winkler, President/Privacy Commission Brazillian Bar Assoc.
talks.teaser: Traces privacy law from a 1890 Harvard article to the EU AI Act, covering biometrics, hiring algorithms and AI training data.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a brief history of privacy, starting with an 1890 Harvard law review article arguing that people should have a right to privacy. It then moves through the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the spread of privacy rules worldwide. The speaker presents the EU's GDPR as the model that shaped many other countries' laws, and describes the United States as a patchwork of state laws without a federal privacy law.

The middle of the talk focuses on AI and biometrics. Examples include facial recognition tools that labelled well-known women as men, applicant tracking software that can reject candidates based on preset settings, a platform that trained AI on user data without clear notice, and Adobe terms of use that claimed rights over creators' work. The speaker also mentions people in China wearing large white masks to evade facial recognition cameras. The EU AI Act's risk tiers are explained, where facial recognition, biometrics and social scoring need a strong legal basis and recruitment counts as high risk.

The closing section looks ahead using a table of disruptive technologies and raises questions about regulating implanted brain devices, such as how they are secured and where their data goes. The main message is that privacy is not a blocker to innovation but a matter of individual control. Practitioners are urged to apply data minimisation and privacy by design, and to keep learning through the books and OECD papers recommended at the end.

talks.title: The Human Factor in Digital Risk, Kate Brett Goldman, CEO & Founder, Cybermaniacs
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding The Human Factor in Digital Risk, Kate Brett Goldman, CEO & Founder, Cybermaniacs.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at CornCon, Kate Goldman (CEO & Founder of Cybermaniacs) discusses the evolving landscape of digital risk and human risk management within organizations. She critiques the traditional framing of employees as "the human firewall" or "the weakest link," arguing instead that human risk must be treated as an inherent part of organizational architecture and measured through behavioral science and organizational anthropology. With shifting regulatory expectations and increasing board-level liability, she highlights the urgent necessity to patch the "human operating system" rather than relying on ineffective annual compliance training.

### Key Topics
- **Cyber Risk as Business and Digital Risk**: Referencing Jen Easterly's congressional testimony, Goldman points out the macro-level strategic transition recognizing that cyber risk is fundamental business risk. Any disruption in people, process, or technology introduces digital risk.
- **Regulatory Pressures and Board Liability**: Citing the Cyber Safety Review Board’s report on Microsoft—which explicitly called Microsoft's security culture "inadequate and requires a complete overhaul"—and new SEC disclosure and oversight rules, Goldman emphasizes that boards are becoming personally and professionally liable for cybersecurity due diligence and risk governance.
- **The Budget and Incident Disparity**: Despite Verizon data breach report figures showing 68% to 87% of security incidents originating from a human cause over the last decade, organizations spend only roughly 2% ($4.5 billion of an estimated $220 billion total cybersecurity spend) addressing the human layer.
- **Critique of the "Human Firewall"**: Expecting regular employees to serve as defensive firewalls against sophisticated cyber adversaries is unrealistic. Employees are natural endpoints who are placed into inherently risky contexts with powerful technology without proper preparation or scoping.

### Technical Details
- **Human Factor Taxonomy**: Goldman defines human-factored digital risk as any action or inaction related to data, information, or technology by a human that directly or indirectly causes or risks harm. She categorizes human factors based on the direction of intention:
  - *Unintentional*: Mistakes, lapses, slips, lack of alignment, missing onboarding, or unaddressed tool navigation gaps.
  - *Intentional*: Policy violations, malicious insider actions, fraud, sabotage, theft, and vandalism.
- **Anthropological Measurement Framework**: Borrowing concepts from industrial and airline safety (such as root cause analysis discussed in Charles Perrow's *Normal Accidents*), Goldman outlines three core organizational dimensions to assess:
  - *Structure*: Evaluating whether decision-making and organization are flat/horizontal or vertical/hierarchical.
  - *Adaptability*: Measuring the organization's agility, responsiveness to change, or risk aversion.
  - *Interdependence*: Assessing collectivism versus individualism in incentives and teamwork.
- **Enabling Cultural Factors**: A mature culture requires leadership prioritization, appropriate resources, group cohesion (notably in mergers and acquisitions), psychological safety to report issues without fear of reprisal, and individual locus of control (fostering personal agency over fatalism).
- **Pitfalls and Dysfunction**: Goldman identifies common cultural blockers to remediation, such as unclear risk tolerance from executive management, fear of delivering bad news, apathy, and overconfidence in IT/security teams.

### Takeaways
- Stop blaming humans as the weakest link; instead, objectively measure and scan for vulnerabilities in the human operating system using behavioral science.
- Build an empowered safety culture characterized by collective risk responsibility, concordance (employee engagement/caring), and high responsiveness/resilience.
- Align cybersecurity oversight with clear corporate risk tolerance, moving beyond surface-level self-attestation checklists and superficial awareness metrics toward rigorous, top-down and bottom-up cultural assessment.

talks.title: Under The Sea: The New Era of Telecommunications, Richard Marshall, Chairman, CinturionGroup
talks.teaser: A veteran attorney surveys how undersea fiber carries most international traffic and what secures new Mediterranean-to-Asia routes.
talks.summary:
Richard Marshall frames global connectivity as communication security, not satellite links alone: he cites figures that nearly all international traffic rides subsea fiber, describes how cables are laid and buried near shore, and lists everyday and adversary threats from fishing gear and anchors to hostile submarines and geopolitical choke points.

He walks through demand drivers such as data centers and AI workloads, then regional fragility—aging Egyptian routes, Iranian pressure near the Strait of Hormuz, and Red Sea disruption that lengthens shipping and blocked a planned cable path. The core of the session is the Centurion build from France and Italy across the Mediterranean, reshaped after the Abraham Accords to include Saudi Arabia, interior links, Corning fiber, guarded landing sites, supply-chain worries about hidden features, and partners for cyber and physical protection.

Practitioners hear why latency and economic growth follow cable paths, how scavenging and sabotage hit terrestrial segments, and why security must be designed in from the start rather than bolted on at landing stations and along desert backhaul.

talks.title: Highly Regulated Industries Panel
talks.teaser: Panelists compare US and EU AI rules and the patchwork of regulation facing security teams in regulated industries.
talks.summary:
A free-form panel led by an attorney moderator brought together three panelists with backgrounds in finance, insurance and state education to discuss regulation of AI and related risk. The discussion began by comparing AI rules in the United States and the European Union. Panelists said US rules are so far sector-specific and driven by consumer protection, with state transparency laws, while the EU has passed a broader AI Act. A US executive order and a federal NIST risk framework were described as early steps.

The middle of the talk focused on model integrity. One panelist noted that financial regulators have overseen statistical models for years, and that bias and inaccuracy in AI models now need similar governance. Security leaders were expected to add change-management style controls, since outsourcing a process does not outsource its risk. A state education example showed student-data contracts that hide backend AI services, and flow-down clauses were proposed for deep vendor chains, though panelists agreed that tracing every party quickly becomes impractical.

The panel closed on open source dependence, citing a backdoor that reached SSH as a reminder that popularity does not guarantee review. They also examined the patchwork of state and federal rules, including an insurance model cybersecurity law adopted unevenly across states, and concluded that the patchwork will persist. For practitioners, the takeaway was to expect new governance duties for AI, third-party risk and identity, and for technical staff to track where regulation is heading.

talks.title: Fielding the Costs: The Economic Challenges of Securing Food Sector, Scott Algeier, Food & Ag-ISAC
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Fielding the Costs: The Economic Challenges of Securing Food Sector, Scott Algeier, Food & Ag-ISAC.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Scott Algeier, Executive Director of the Food and Agriculture Information Sharing and Analysis Center (Food & Ag-ISAC) and the IT-ISAC, examines the asymmetric economics of cybersecurity and their direct impact on the food and agriculture critical infrastructure sector. Modern agriculture increasingly incorporates technology to feed larger populations on fewer acres, expanding its overall attack surface. While defenders incur mounting expenses across tooling, staffing, and compliance mandates, cyber adversaries benefit from low operational costs, lucrative payouts, and collaborative networks. Algeier advocates for industry-wide threat intelligence sharing and collaboration through ISACs to pool defense resources and counter threat actors.

### Key Topics
- **Formation and Role of the Food & Ag-ISAC**: Launched in May 2023 in partnership with the IT-ISAC (established in 2000), the Food & Ag-ISAC addresses risks spanning "pre-farm to table"—from seed research to consumer distribution. By partnering with IT-ISAC, it leveraged existing infrastructure rather than spending a decade building analytic capabilities independently.
- **Economic Asymmetry Between Attackers and Defenders**: Attacking remains cheap, with cybercriminals offering ransomware-as-a-service for as little as $40 per month, malware installation starting around $35, and DDoS tools for modest fees. In contrast, global defense spending reaches $215 billion annually, businesses spend 10–15% of IT budgets on security (~$2,700 per full-time employee), and average breach recovery costs hit $4.88 million in 2024. Despite this spending, global cybercrime damages are estimated at $9.5 trillion in 2024, projected to exceed $10 trillion in 2025.
- **Regulatory Pressure and Resource Diversion**: Proliferation of compliance and mandatory incident reporting frameworks (including SEC rules and proposed CISA requirements added to 36 existing federal reporting rules) often diverts fixed security budgets toward legal and compliance overhead, with some firms employing three to four compliance personnel per security defender.

### Technical Details
- **Incident Breakdown in Food and Agriculture**: Incident tracking indicates that ransomware accounts for over 53% of observed incidents, followed by nation-state actors at 27%, alongside hacktivists and other cybercriminals.
- **Nation-State and APT Threats**: Advanced persistent threat actors prioritize cyber espionage and intellectual property theft. Algeier notes that developing corn seed technology can require $30 to $40 million in laboratory testing over seven years, making R&D a prime target for nation-states (such as China) seeking to bypass domestic R&D costs via network compromise or biological theft. Additionally, nations such as North Korea leverage cyber operations for state funding, while critical infrastructure dependencies (such as power and energy) create operational risks.
- **Ransomware Tracking & Metrics**: Food & Ag-ISAC tracks over 6,500 historical ransomware incidents since 2020. In 2023, 167 out of over 3,000 tracked critical infrastructure attacks targeted food and agriculture (5.5%). In the first half of 2024, 80 out of 1,000 critical infrastructure attacks were in food and agriculture (~7%), with overall incidents temporarily dipping due to law enforcement disruptions. While attackers rarely target the sector exclusively, just-in-time delivery supply chains increase pressure to pay higher ransoms once an organization is compromised.

### Takeaways
- **Defend Collaboratively**: Because cybercriminals collaborate, share playbooks, and mentor each other, isolated defense is economically unsustainable. Food & Ag-ISAC provides vendor-neutral threat reporting, hunting platforms, and adversary attack playbooks mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework across 250+ threat actors.
- **Divide and Conquer**: Member enterprises can distribute threat monitoring responsibilities across peer analysts to avoid redundant workloads.
- **Voluntary Sharing Outperforms Regulation**: Reporting incidents to government agencies under mandatory compliance rules does not provide operational defense assistance, as federal entities like CISA lack resources to protect individual corporate networks. Voluntary peer collaboration serves as a more practical force multiplier.

talks.title: The Ultimate List of Top 10s, Chris Roberts, Deepfake Cyber Strategist, World Wide Technolgy
talks.teaser: Walks through deepfake signal analysis, questions to ask vendors and employers, and simple mental health habits for security staff.
talks.summary:
This closing keynote-style talk is built as a run through a series of "top 10" lists about security, with the speaker arguing that practitioners often skip the basic questions, both for themselves and when helping others. He opens with AI-generated images to show how convincing fakes have become, including a black-and-white landscape photo made from a short training run and about 30 seconds of generation, and argues that spotting deepfakes by eye will not last.

In the middle section he proposes treating deepfakes as signals. Defenders would look at text, audio, visual, social media and real-time channels, ask where a call or message is coming from, enrich that data, work out who is actually speaking, and check what the other party wants. He cites roughly 10 billion US dollars lost to fraud last year and says a feedback loop is needed to learn what was missed. The talk then moves to managed service providers, where he stresses accountability and understanding the customer's business, and to tabletop exercises, which he says can run in a single coffee or lunch break. He also gives questions to ask a prospective employer about security posture, top concerns, risk appetite and incident response plans, plus a short list of vendor claims to challenge.

The closing section covers mental health habits such as journaling, finishing one small task a day, making the bed, and stepping away from technology. He ends with a call to teach people to ask the right questions and to push back on anyone who says their product solves everything.
